raw_response.adversarial_critique:
Adversarial audit of S358 (Williams et al., 2025) identifies both material extraction/specification discrepancies in `effect_sizes.csv` (indicating Abstract-only extraction) and a clear scope inconsistency under the CK A24/A26/A28 eligibility standard (`E04`).

1. Extraction & Statistical Discrepancies in `effect_sizes.csv`: While the stored point estimates (`OR = 0.62, p < 0.001` for Tribal primacy; `OR = 2.01` for % Black and `OR = 0.92` for % Hispanic/Latino, `p < 0.001`) match the Abstract (PDF p. 1), the stored row leaves `standard_error`, `lower_CI` and `upper_CI` blank even though Table 2 (PDF p. 16) prints the exact regression coefficient and standard error (`est. = −0.484, SE = 0.008, Statistic = −57.086`, derivable 95% CI `[0.61, 0.63]`). Worse, `adjusted` falsely claims that `OR = 0.62` controls for race/ethnicity, gender, age 65+, household/family structure and institutional/migrant-worker housing. Inspection of the regression tables shows that `OR = 0.62` comes from the 20-year binary Arsenic + Water Policy model in Table 2 (controlling only for binary arsenic detection/exceedance, GMA NDA status, karst aquifer and DWA supply type; in the parallel Nitrate model in Table 2, Tribal primacy is `OR = 0.84`, not `0.62`), whereas `OR = 2.01` and `OR = 0.92` come from the separate continuous-nitrate specification in Table 3 / Table A1 (PDF pp. 17, 25), where `SDWA Primacy (Tribal)` has reversed positive linear estimates (`6.621, SE = 0.684` and `8.103, SE = 0.330`). Moreover, `exposure_definition` conflates federal Safe Drinking Water Act public-system oversight (`SDWA Primacy (Tribal)`) with groundwater withdrawal regulation (`GMA Designation (NDA)`), `outcome_family` mislabels physical subbasin water-table depletion as `effective_access`, and `sample_size` cites the `1,881` mapped service areas without noting that the regressions were estimated on unclustered water-quality sample datasets (`27,334` arsenic and `47,783` nitrate observations, PDF p. 9), producing severely deflated standard errors (`SE = 0.006–0.009`).

2. Internal Reporting Defects in the Source Paper: Williams et al. (2025) mislabel exponentiated odds ratios `exp(est.)` as `Log Odds` in Table 2; exponentiate continuous linear water-level coefficients (`ft/year`) in Table 3 into meaningless `Log Odds` values (`6.27E+39` for arsenic, `3305.44` and `751.01` for Tribal primacy) with unexplained sign reversals relative to Table 2; and copy Table 3's continuous-model slopes into Tables A1–A2 while mislabeling the response footnote as a binary decline variable (`1 = decline`).

3. Non-Fit Verdict vs Review Scope Eligibility (`E04`): Conditional on keeping S358 in the review, CK's A26 decision to remove it from Family A (`reasoned non-fit`) would be fully justified because no SWiM family pools physical aquifer water-table elevation (`ft/year`). However, that very A26 rationale (`the outcome is groundwater decline and contamination risk at the level of 1,881 groundwater-supplied service areas (aquifer availability), not household connection, access or service quality`) establishes that S358 fails Criterion 4 (`E04` hydrological/environmental resource state). Although the authors apply the conceptual label `access` to regulatory and Census predictors, all four regression tables model subbasin ADWR index-well water-level change—which is not even a monotonic proxy for safe drinking water because rising/stabilizing water levels mobilize arsenic and nitrate (`OR = 1.01` and `1.05, p < 0.001`, PDF p. 15). Nor can the un-tabulated text mentions of `MCLExceeded` (PDF p. 15) rescue eligibility: no Tribal-primacy point estimate or SE is reported for `MCLExceeded`, and the underlying contamination dataset mixes EPA CWS compliance records with USGS/ADEQ private/ambient groundwater samples (`97.8%` of arsenic below MDL). Under the same CK scope standard that excluded non-household outcomes (e.g. `S1121`), S358 should be flagged for PI exclusion under `E04`, rendering SWiM family assignment moot.

raw_response.number_verification_detail: Discrepancies found between `effect_sizes.csv` and the full text (indicating Abstract-only extraction): (1) Point estimates `OR=0.62, p<0.001` (Tribal primacy), `OR=2.01, p<0.001` (% Black) and `OR=0.92, p<0.001` (% Hispanic/Latino) match the Abstract (PDF p. 1), Table 2 (PDF p. 16) and Table A1 (PDF p. 25), and `1,881` matches the mapped service-area count (PDF pp. 1, 8). (2) Omitted SE and derivable CI: `standard_error`, `lower_CI` and `upper_CI` are left blank in `effect_sizes.csv`, whereas Table 2 (PDF p. 16, 20-Year GWL Arsenic binary model) explicitly prints `est. = −0.484`, `Std Error = 0.008`, `Statistic = −57.086`, `p < 0.001`, `OR = 0.62` (mislabeled `Log Odds` in the table header; `exp(−0.484) = 0.616`, 95% CI `[0.61, 0.63]`). In the companion 20-Year GWL Nitrate binary model in Table 2, `SDWA Primacy (Tribal)` is `OR = 0.84` (`est. = −0.173, SE = 0.017`), and 10-Year ORs are `0.69` (Arsenic) and `0.89` (Nitrate). (3) Conflated covariate adjustment (`adjusted` field): `effect_sizes.csv` states that `OR = 0.62` came from a multivariate regression controlling for race/ethnicity, gender, age 65+, household/family structure, institutional/migrant-worker housing and designated-management-area status. In reality, Table 2's `OR = 0.62` model includes ONLY binary arsenic (`Detect`, `MCL Exceeded`) and four policy/hydrogeology indicators (`GMA Designation (NDA)`, `SDWA Primacy (Tribal)`, `Aquifer Type (Karst)`, `Supply Type (DWA)`), whereas the demographic/housing ORs (`2.01` for Black, `0.92` for Hispanic/Latino) come from Table 3 / Table A1 (PDF pp. 17, 25, 20-Year continuous Nitrate model), where `SDWA Primacy (Tribal)` has a reversed positive linear slope `est. = 6.621, SE = 0.684` (improperly exponentiated as `751.01`, and `8.103, SE = 0.330` / `3305.44` in the Arsenic model). (4) Effective sample size: while `1,881` service areas were mapped, the tiny SEs (`0.006–0.009`) show regressions were fit at the contaminant-sample level (`27,334` arsenic and `47,783` nitrate observations, PDF p. 9) rather than `N = 1,881` service areas. (5) Exposure/outcome misdescription: `SDWA Primacy (Tribal)` is Safe Drinking Water Act public-water-system primacy rather than GMA groundwater withdrawal jurisdiction, and `outcome_family = effective_access` contradicts the physical subbasin aquifer decline dependent variable.
